Welcome Back: The Quantum Advantage

Last time, we talked about why we even bother looking into this whole quantum photon mumbo jumbo. On one hand, we have our handy classical bits—the ones up in the cloud, on our cell phones, and in our laptops. At the end of the day, each of those classical bits only stores one single value: a 1 or a 0.

But we saw that if we have a quantum version of those bits—what we call qubits—the game changes entirely. One qubit stores two numbers at the same time. Put two qubits together, and you are storing four numbers simultaneously. Three qubits store eight values, and so on. We saw that we only needed something like 50 qubits to store a quadrillion values—a number millions of times greater than the world population! In a nutshell, that is why people are going gaga over quantum computing.

Over the next couple of lectures, I want us to go over the stuff that makes qubits weird and, in a way, somewhat non-intuitive. But as your coach, I am going to try to make it as intuitive as possible, and show you how it is actually useful.

The Language of Quantum States

Let’s quickly review. A quantum bit, or quantum state, is built on a magic phrase: superposition (or linear combination). That is a big phrase that makes us sound like big people coming out of this class!

To understand superposition, I am going to throw three more big words at you: orthonormal, basis, and states. We will break these down in a moment, but first, let’s look at how we write a superposition.

A quantum state is a linear combination of two basis states. For our purposes, we are looking specifically at the direction of photon polarization. We will define our two foundational states as:

  • 0 \equiv a photon that is polarized horizontally.

  • 1 \equiv a photon that is polarized vertically.

We don’t just add these states together straight out; we attach a little coefficient in front of each. These coefficients are called probability amplitudes.

You will notice I always use this strange half-bracket thingy: |\cdot\rangle. This is called ket notation (part of the larger "bra-ket" notation used in physics and chemistry). For this class, we are mostly just going to deal with the "ket." Let’s define our quantum state, |\psi\rangle, using these probability amplitudes, which we will call a_0 and a_1:

\begin{equation} \tag{1} |\psi\rangle = a_0 |H\rangle + a_1 |V\rangle \end{equation}

Here, |H\rangle represents the horizontal state and |V\rangle represents the vertical state.

Vector Notation

What is probably more useful for us is to write this in a slightly different way. From pre-calc or physics, you have all seen vectors. We can write this superposition in vector notation. Our horizontal and vertical states can be represented as column vectors:

\begin{equation} \tag{2} |H\rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad |V\rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}

So, our quantum state vector looks like this:

\begin{equation} \tag{3} |\psi\rangle = \begin{pmatrix} a_0 \\ a_1 \end{pmatrix} = a_0 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + a_1 \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}

This makes it very intuitive. The top number (a_0) represents the horizontal component, and the bottom number (a_1) represents the vertical component. The vector \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} is entirely horizontal (zero vertical), and \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} is entirely vertical (zero horizontal).

Deconstructing "Orthonormal Basis States"

Now, back to those three big words: orthonormal basis states.

  • Ortho means perpendicular (orthogonal). Our horizontal and vertical vectors are definitely perpendicular to each other.

  • Normal means having a length of 1. If you go one unit horizontally or one unit vertically, the length is obviously 1.

  • Basis means building blocks. By linearly combining these two vectors, you can draw any polarization direction you want.

To make this even more intuitive, let’s look at some analogies: 1. 3D Space: In physics, you describe any position or velocity in 3D space by linearly combining the X, Y, and Z unit vectors. Those three vectors form an orthonormal basis. 2. Video Game Characters: If you play RPGs, your character has attributes like strength, speed, endurance, and magic. These are like basis vectors. You can build any character by linearly combining different amounts of these attributes. 3. Cooking: Think about the basic elements of taste: salty, sweet, sour, bitter, and umami. You cannot get "sweet" out of "salty" (just like you cannot get vertical out of horizontal). But by linearly combining these basic tastes, you can create any flavor profile you want!

Expanding Our Horizons: Alternative Bases

So, any photon state is a linear combination of horizontal and vertical. We call this the standard orthonormal basis because it is the easiest thing to picture.

But why limit ourselves to horizontal and vertical? What if we used 45^\circ (which I’ll call "up-diagonal") and -45^\circ (which I’ll call "down-diagonal")?

Is there anything wrong with writing our photon state that way? Not at all! The 45^\circ and -45^\circ directions are perpendicular to each other, and we can adjust their lengths so they are exactly 1. This is an entirely legit way to write a photon state.

Let’s define this new 45^\circ / -45^\circ orthonormal basis. Using our unit circle knowledge, an angle of 45^\circ has equal horizontal and vertical components. To keep the length at 1, those components must be \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.

\begin{align} |45^\circ\rangle &= \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{pmatrix} \label{eq:up_diag} \\ |-45^\circ\rangle &= \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{pmatrix} \tag{4} \end{align}

Let’s verify that these are "normal" (length of 1) using our good old Pythagorean theorem. The length is the square root of the horizontal component squared plus the vertical component squared:

\begin{equation} \text{Length of } |45^\circ\rangle = \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{1} = 1 \tag{5} \end{equation}

It works! The same math applies to the down-diagonal state. You don’t have to limit yourself to horizontal and vertical; you can linearly combine up-diagonal and down-diagonal states to make up any polarization vector you want. You could even use a 60^\circ and -30^\circ basis if you wanted to. There are an infinite number of possibilities.

The Weirdness of Measurement

Okay, so why does it matter that we can write a photon state in a variety of different ways?

You have probably heard that in quantum mechanics, what you get out of a measurement depends on how you measure the thing. This basis stuff is the natural way to explain that.

In a nutshell: when you do a measurement, you are automatically picking which basis you are in.

Let’s look at an example. If I take a polarizer and set it horizontally, there are only two outcomes for a single photon: 1. The photon comes through \rightarrow it is 100\% horizontal (|H\rangle). 2. The photon is blocked \rightarrow it is 100\% vertical (|V\rangle).

That isn’t too weird. But what if I shoot that exact same horizontal photon at a polarizer set to 45^\circ?

I know the photon coming in is horizontal. But I am not going to get a horizontal or vertical photon out the other side. If the photon comes through, it has to be oriented at 45^\circ. If it doesn’t come through, it has to be -45^\circ.

So what happens? There is a 50/50 split.

As shown in the sketch above, if we send a horizontal photon (|H\rangle) into a 45^\circ polarizer:

  • There is a 50\% chance it will come through. If it does, it is now a |45^\circ\rangle photon.

  • There is a 50\% chance it is blocked. This means it collapsed into the state perpendicular to the polarizer, which is |-45^\circ\rangle.

By setting the polarizer in a specific direction, we limit the outcomes we can see. The measurement itself automatically sets the possible outcomes. Mathematically speaking, by setting our measurement, we are setting the possible basis states.

Collapsing the Superposition

Here is another weird thing: a 45^\circ oriented photon is a superposition (an even mix) of vertical and horizontal.

\begin{equation} |45^\circ\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} |H\rangle + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} |V\rangle \tag{6} \end{equation}

But you can never actually see this superposition directly. As soon as you try to measure or "see" the superposition, you disturb it. It collapses to one of the two basis states of your measurement device.

If you pass that |45^\circ\rangle photon through a horizontal polarizer, you will only see vertical or horizontal. The probability of getting one of these states is the probability amplitude squared.

For our |45^\circ\rangle photon hitting a horizontal polarizer, the amplitude for horizontal is \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}. \begin{equation} \text{Probability of passing (Horizontal)} = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} = 50\% \tag{7} \end{equation}

It sounds strange, and you might start thinking this superposition stuff is useless because we can’t actually see it. But trust me, we will look at cases where it becomes incredibly useful soon.

Visualizing Transmission Probabilities

Let’s systematically walk through how different incident photons behave when they hit different polarizers. We will look at four scenarios.

Scenario 1: The Horizontal Polarizer

Here, our measurement basis is the standard horizontal/vertical basis. The polarizer is set to 0^\circ (horizontal).

If a photon is already aligned with the polarizer (0^\circ), its amplitude is 1, and 1^2 = 100\% probability of transmission. If it is perpendicular (90^\circ), its amplitude is 0, so it is blocked. If it is diagonal, it is an even mix of horizontal and vertical, so it has a 50\% chance of passing.

Scenario 2: The Vertical Polarizer

Now we rotate the polarizer by 90^\circ so it is vertical. We are still in the standard basis, just measuring the other component.

The results flip! The horizontal photon is blocked (0\%), the vertical photon passes (100\%), and the diagonal photons still have a 50\% chance of passing because they contain equal parts horizontal and vertical. Notice that for the -45^\circ photon, the vertical amplitude is -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}. When we square it to find the probability, the negative sign goes away: \left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = 50\%.

Scenario 3: The Up-Diagonal Polarizer

Now we change our measurement device to the diagonal basis, setting the polarizer to 45^\circ.

Because the polarizer is at 45^\circ, an incoming 45^\circ photon passes flawlessly (100\%). An incoming -45^\circ photon is orthogonal to the polarizer, so it is blocked (0\%). The horizontal and vertical photons are now the ones that are "mixed" relative to this basis, so they each have a 50\% chance of passing.

Scenario 4: The Down-Diagonal Polarizer

Finally, we set the polarizer to -45^\circ.

As expected, the -45^\circ photon passes (100\%), the 45^\circ photon is blocked (0\%), and the standard horizontal/vertical photons each have a 50\% chance of making it through.

Testing Our Intuition: The Polarizer Game

To wrap up, we played a little game in class to test our intuition on this. We had a "referee" setting a polarizer angle, and a "measurer" predicting the transmission probability of an incoming photon.

If the incoming photon is lined up exactly with the polarizer, you get 100\% transmission. If it is perpendicular, you get 0\%. If it is 45^\circ off from the polarizer, you get 50\%.

But what if we make it harder? What if the incoming photon is at 30^\circ and the polarizer is horizontal (0^\circ)?

We can figure this out using the unit circle. The horizontal component of a 30^\circ angle is \cos(30^\circ) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}. That is our probability amplitude. To get the actual probability of transmission, we square the amplitude:

\begin{equation} \text{Probability} = \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{3}{4} = 75\% \tag{8} \end{equation}

So a 30^\circ photon has a 75\% chance of passing through a horizontal polarizer!

For the purposes of this class, if you can confidently predict the outcomes for 0^\circ, 90^\circ, 45^\circ, and -45^\circ, you are in great shape. That is going to allow us to talk about some really weird stuff next time—specifically, a concept called entanglement.

I encourage everybody to come out next time. We are going to learn about entanglement through candy! See you then.
